findings.finding: The plan doesn't specify how old and new rebar versions coexist on the same store. The production bridge on main will write the new release delta and release-bearing SNAPSHOTs, while developers' older CLIs keep reading and writing that store. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a rollout/rollback clause and AC: upgrade the reconcile host first (per docs/event-schema.md). State how a release delta buried by an older binary's SNAPSHOT is detected and recovered (fsck WARN / orphan repair), and pin with a test that compaction by an old-version compactor followed by replay on the new version still yields the correct `releases` (or is flagged and repairable).
evidence: Plan: 'Older stores replay unchanged, and older readers ignore the field under the schema forward-compatibility rules in `docs/event-schema.md`.' This covers reading only, not compaction by an older binary.
src/rebar/_commands/compact_txn.py:268: candidates are filtered to `c.is_known_type`, so an older binary excludes the unknown delta from old/young.
compact_txn._snapshot_timestamp: `snapshot_ts = max(old_ts) + 1`, computed over known-type events only.
src/rebar/reducer/_replay.py:140,161: `start_idx = latest_snapshot_idx` and `if idx < start_idx: continue`, so any event before the latest SNAPSHOT is skipped unless the SNAPSHOT cites it.
docs/event-schema.md 'Detectability + rollout': 'Deployment rule: upgrade reconciler-running clones FIRST'. The plan does not adopt or cite this rule.
No AC pins state after a rollback or a compaction by an older binary.
findings.finding: The plan relies on 'older readers ignore the field under the schema forward-compatibility rules' but says nothing about older clones that compact while the new release delta event is in the store. An older binary treats the new delta as an unknown type and leaves it out of the fold, then writes a SNAPSHOT just after its newest known event. If any release delta sorts before that SNAPSHOT, newer clones skip it on replay. The file is kept, but its releases silently disappear from compiled state. Outbound sync could then remove those values from Jira fixVersions, or they could stay lost until fsck repair. The plan sets no rollout order (reconcile host first), gives no guidance for rollback or mixed-version clones, and has no test for what state looks like after a rollback.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Store and reducer' and the Constraints section (no rollout/rollback clause); AC 'Compiled ticket state carries the release field…'
scenarios: The reconcile host is upgraded and writes inbound release deltas. A developer clone still on the old version then runs `rebar compact` on that ticket after a later EDIT. The new SNAPSHOT sorts after the delta, and upgraded clones now show empty releases.

The bridge deploy is rolled back after release deltas exist. The old host's compaction buries them, and after re-upgrade the outbound diff sees no local releases, so Jira values in the ever-seen intent set may be removed.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach step 2 (and the ADR), add: 'Rollout: upgrade reconciler-running clones first; fsck WARNs on the new event type for older binaries. A release delta left uncited before an older clone's SNAPSHOT is an ORPHAN_EVENT recovered by `fsck --repair-snapshots`; outbound fixVersions removal is suppressed while fsck reports such orphans.' Add an AC test: simulate a pre-upgrade compaction (known types excluding the new delta), then reduce with the new binary and assert the releases are either preserved or flagged as repairable orphans.

findings.finding: The plan adds a new failure-handling arm (an outbound fixVersions write that fails, then alert and retry every pass). It states a disposition only for the 'version missing' case. Five things are left without a stated disposition. (1) How 'missing version' is told apart from other write failures, such as permission denied, field not settable on a Data Center screen, or archived version, and whether those are permanent (alert, no retry) or transient (retry). (2) Whether one missing version blocks the other release adds/removes, or the ticket's other outbound fields, in the same pass. (3) The disposition for archived and deleted versions, which is deferred to the ADR without stating fatal vs retryable. (4) How the retry-forever value survives the inbound set-diff. Jira will keep lacking the release, so `_diff_labels_inbound`-style logic could treat it as a Jira-side removal and delete it from rebar. (5) How an alert raised on a non-missing failure resolves.

findings.finding: The missing-version rule ('the release stays on the rebar ticket… each pass retries') contradicts the inbound mechanism the plan prescribes. The plan says inbound follows `_diff_labels_inbound`, a plain set-diff that emits a REMOVE for every local value absent from Jira. A withheld release is local-only and never written to Jira, so the next inbound pass will remove it from the rebar ticket. For labels the same-pass outbound ADD hides this, because bidirectional suppression drops the matching inbound REMOVE. A withheld release produces no outbound ADD, so nothing suppresses the REMOVE. The plan names no guard for this.

scenarios: A user sets release '2.4' in rebar before anyone creates version 2.4 in Jira. The outbound pass withholds it.
